text:
GREEN FUEL & SUSTENTABILITY

Portbiz | International Ports and Logistics

It is colourless, corrosive, toxic at concentrations that can be measured in parts per million, and it burns with a stubbornness that has defeated centuries of conventional engineering. It is also, by a growing consensus among regulators, shipowners, and engine manufacturers, the most serious candidate to decarbonise the deep-sea shipping that carries 80 per cent of global trade by volume. This is the contradiction at the heart of ammonia's maritime moment.

On a June morning in 2026, a 46,000 cubic metre gas carrier named Antwerpen sailed out of a South Korean shipyard and into the record books. The vessel, delivered to Belgian shipowner Exmar, was the first ocean-going ship to be powered by a dual-fuel ammonia engine built by WinGD, the Swiss marine engine developer whose ammonia orderbook has now crossed 40 units across gas carriers, bulkers, tankers, and container ships. Carl-Antoine Saverys, CEO of the Exmar Group, spoke plainly about what the delivery represented. Ammonia propulsion, he said, was no longer theoretical. The industry was deploying it.

That statement, coming from an operator rather than a technology developer, carries weight that a product launch announcement does not. And yet the Antwerpen's departure also clarified how much remains unresolved: the global bunkering infrastructure for ammonia barely exists at scale; the fuel costs between two and three times as much as the conventional oil products it would replace; the regulatory framework that would make the economics viable is still being contested between governments; and the safety challenges of handling a substance acutely toxic at concentrations far below what the human nose can reliably detect have not been fully answered at the operational level.

The ammonia gamble is real, the stakes are high, and the timeline is closing.

Why the Industry Has No Better Option

To understand why a fuel this difficult has become the focus of so much investment and regulatory energy, it is necessary to understand what the alternatives are not.

Shipping accounts for approximately 3 per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions. That figure, modest in isolation, represents around one billion tonnes of CO₂ equivalent per year, produced by a sector that powers the physical infrastructure of the global economy. The International Maritime Organization's net-zero framework, adopted in principle in April 2025 and scheduled for implementation from 2027, requires shipping to reach net-zero emissions by 2050, with interim targets of 20 per cent reduction by 2030 and 70 per cent by 2040. The EU's FuelEU Maritime regulation, already in force since January 2025, imposes progressively stricter greenhouse gas intensity requirements on vessels calling European ports, with penalties reaching approximately €2,400 per tonne of VLSFO energy equivalent for non-compliance.

Against those targets, the current fuel mix offers almost nothing. Heavy fuel oil and very low sulphur fuel oil, which together account for around 75 per cent of global bunker consumption, emit approximately 3 kilogrammes of CO₂-equivalent per kilogramme of fuel consumed. LNG, which has grown its bunkering market share from 1 per cent to 4 per cent between 2019 and 2026, reduces sulphur and particulate emissions meaningfully but delivers almost no carbon benefit on a well-to-wake basis once methane slip through the value chain is accounted for.

Biofuels are available now, but their feedstock base is limited and will face competition from aviation, chemicals, and food production that will constrain their scale. Green methanol has attracted significant newbuild orders from major carriers including Maersk and CMA CGM, and its liquid form at ambient temperature makes it easier to handle and store than either hydrogen or ammonia. But green methanol depends on sustainable sources of carbon dioxide alongside green hydrogen, and as the heavy industries that currently produce point-source CO₂ decarbonise, that supply will shrink. At scale and over the long term, methanol faces a carbon supply constraint that its advocates have not fully answered.

Batteries and hydrogen fuel cells offer genuine zero-emission solutions for ferries, tugs, and harbour craft on short routes with frequent charging or bunkering opportunities. For vessels crossing the Pacific or rounding the Cape of Good Hope, the energy density mathematics are prohibitive. Batteries currently carry roughly twenty times less energy per unit of mass than ammonia or methanol, and fifty times less than conventional marine fuel. That gap does not close with foreseeable battery technology development.

Ammonia, by contrast, is a liquid at moderate pressure and manageable temperatures. It can be stored and transported in infrastructure that already exists at scale, since the fertiliser industry ships approximately 17 million tonnes of ammonia globally each year through a network of around 170 terminals worldwide. It produces no carbon dioxide when combusted. It can be produced from renewable electricity, water, and nitrogen, ingredients that are geographically distributed and theoretically inexhaustible. And its engines, as the Antwerpen demonstrated, now work at commercial scale.

The case for ammonia is not that it is easy. It is that nothing else scales.

The Physics of Difficulty

Ammonia is acutely toxic. Its immediately dangerous to life and health concentration — the threshold at which a 30-minute exposure causes irreversible harm — is 300 parts per million. By comparison, the human olfactory system detects ammonia at around 5 parts per million, which means that meaningful warning precedes dangerous exposure, but also that the margin between detectability and serious harm is narrower than crew training programmes have historically needed to address with conventional fuels.

A UK P&I Club analysis published in July 2026 identified the primary failure modes during bunkering with clinical precision: hose failures during fuel transfer; incorrect valve alignment; physical damage to fuel tanks or piping; and, most severely, vessel collisions capable of rupturing onboard storage tanks. A quantitative risk study of ammonia bunkering operations by Chinese maritime researchers, published in 2026, found that human error accounted for 45 per cent of identified risk events during ammonia transfers, with the risk priority number for technical malfunctions during transfers reaching 378, the highest category in their failure mode analysis. Virtual reality training that improved crew performance by 41 per cent in simulations was among the recommended risk controls.

Between 1978 and 2021, twelve grave accidents involving ammonia transport on LPG carriers were recorded, resulting in fatalities. Those events occurred in an era of more limited safety engineering and before the dedicated training, monitoring, and emergency response protocols that ammonia-as-fuel operations now require. But they establish a baseline of real-world consequence that the industry cannot bracket as theoretical.

The toxicity risk is not limited to the vessel. An ammonia release during bunkering in a busy port affects crew, dock workers, and potentially the surrounding urban environment. Simulation studies conducted for the Port of Singapore modelled large-scale ammonia releases during ship-to-ship bunkering operations under various weather conditions and found that the behaviour of ammonia over water and on land is substantially affected by atmospheric parameters in ways that make consequence modelling complex. Semi-pressurised storage tanks, the configuration common on many existing gas carriers, were found to present greater health risk in accident scenarios than fully refrigerated configurations, because the pressure differential accelerates initial release rates.

Beyond toxicity, ammonia combustion presents its own engineering challenges. Its ignition temperature is high, its flammability range narrow, and its flame speed slow, all properties that make it stubbornly reluctant to burn efficiently in a conventional engine. MAN Energy Solutions and WinGD have both addressed this through dual-fuel designs that use a small pilot quantity of conventional fuel, approximately 5 per cent by energy at full load, to initiate and stabilise combustion. The approach works, as the Antwerpen's sea trials demonstrated, with fuel efficiency comparable to equivalent diesel-fuelled engines. But the residual pilot fuel dependency means that ammonia-powered vessels are not quite zero-emission in practice, and the nitrogen chemistry of ammonia combustion generates nitrogen oxides as a byproduct, requiring aftertreatment systems to prevent a new emission problem from replacing the old one.

IMO discussions at PPR 13 in 2026 specifically addressed the management of ammonia effluents, a signal that regulators are beginning to grapple with the full environmental profile of the fuel rather than simply its carbon credentials.

The Orderbook Is Moving

Despite these challenges, the industry is not waiting for the problems to be fully resolved before committing capital.

WinGD's ammonia engine orderbook crossing 40 units in the first half of 2026 is one data point among many. Hapag-Lloyd has 12 ammonia-ready newbuilds on order. Rio Tinto and AngloEastern are developing Newcastlemax-class ammonia-powered bulk carriers. Eastern Pacific Shipping has ordered ammonia-powered Newcastlemaxes and a very large ammonia carrier fleet for delivery from 2026 onwards. NYK, Mitsui OSK Lines, and a series of Greek tonnage owners including TMS Cardiff Gas and Capital Maritime have added ammonia carrier orders to their fleets. Maersk Tankers, whose parent A.P. Moller Holding controls the container shipping giant, has 10 very large ammonia carriers on order, with the first, the Jane Maersk, delivered in 2026 as the first such vessel built by HD Hyundai Samho.

The Ammonia Energy Association estimates that approximately 140 ammonia-powered vessels are currently on the global orderbook, with the majority of deliveries scheduled for 2026 and 2027. That number remains a small fraction of a global fleet of roughly 100,000 ships, but the concentration of newbuild commitment in this two-year window reflects a technology reaching its commercial inflection point rather than a market still exploring feasibility.

COSCO completed the world's first green ammonia bunkering operation in 2025, a milestone whose significance lies less in the volumes involved than in the demonstration that the operational chain, from production to storage to transfer to combustion, can work under real conditions. Multiple large-scale ship-to-ship ammonia transfers were completed between 2024 and 2025, including operations exceeding 25,000 tonnes, serving as operational proxies for bunkering and providing the procedural experience that safety protocols require.

On the engine side, MAN Energy Solutions is delivering its ammonia-capable ME-LGIA two-stroke engines with 80-bore configurations targeted for commercial availability by end of 2026. Wärtsilä is developing four-stroke ammonia engines for applications including smaller vessels and dual-fuel conversions. Classification societies including Lloyd's Register, DNV, Bureau Veritas, and the China Classification Society have all issued approval in principle for ammonia-fuelled vessel designs, creating the regulatory foundation for insurance and financing.

The Cost Gap and How It Closes

The economic case for ammonia is not yet self-sustaining, and honesty about that matters for any assessment of the transition's timeline.

As of mid-2026, green ammonia produced from renewable electricity costs between $800 and $1,200 per tonne on an equivalent energy basis, compared with VLSFO at approximately $600 per tonne. Because ammonia has a lower energy density than conventional marine fuel, a ship requires roughly 2.4 times the volume of ammonia to achieve the same range, meaning the total fuel cost gap is not simply the price-per-tonne differential. A green ammonia-powered voyage on a comparable distance may cost between three and four times more in fuel alone than the same voyage on conventional oil.

Production costs are expected to decline. Green ammonia production is projected to fall from approximately €634 per tonne in 2025 to around €380 per tonne by 2040 as electrolyser deployment scales and renewable electricity costs continue their structural decline. Envision Energy's ammonia facility in Chifeng, China, is already producing around 320,000 tonnes per year with exports having begun in late 2025, and production capacity at that facility alone is projected to reach 1.5 million tonnes annually by 2028. A joint study by WinGD and Envision published in March 2026 found that under a moderate global regulatory regime, green ammonia could reach cost parity with VLSFO and LNG by 2050, with a projected 5 to 6 per cent lower lifecycle cost than LNG over the long term.

What bridges the gap between now and 2050 is regulation. The IMO's two-tier carbon pricing framework, scheduled to impose a base levy of $100 per tonne of CO₂ and a higher penalty of $380 per tonne for vessels exceeding stricter emission thresholds from 2028, will begin to change the relative economics of fuel choice in ways that pure market pricing does not. The EU ETS, already applying full coverage to shipping from 2026 at carbon prices in the mid-€60s per tonne with projections pointing to €105 by 2027, adds further cost to conventional fuel operations on European-touching routes. FuelEU Maritime penalties of approximately €2,400 per tonne of VLSFO equivalent will make non-compliance increasingly expensive as the greenhouse gas intensity requirements tighten through 2030 and beyond.

The H2Global mechanism, supported by the German Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Climate Action, is providing up to €3 billion in its second funding round through contracts for difference that offer long-term price certainty for green hydrogen derivative producers. A dedicated shipping-sector tranche of H2Global is being prepared to insulate maritime ammonia offtake from direct competition with other end-use sectors during the transition. The European Hydrogen Bank, Japan's contract-for-difference schemes, and various national green shipping subsidy programmes are complementing this support architecture.

The Ammonia Energy Association estimates that approximately 2.5 million tonnes per year of renewable ammonia production capacity will be available by 2028, more than double the estimated fuel demand of the roughly 53 ammonia-powered ships scheduled for delivery by that date. In the immediate commercial window, fuel availability is not the binding constraint.

The Port Infrastructure Gap

The Antwerpen can sail. What it cannot easily do, in most of the world's major commercial ports, is refuel without significant advance coordination.

Dedicated ammonia bunkering infrastructure at commercial scale remains limited. The 170 ammonia terminals that serve the fertiliser industry are distributed across major industrial ports and provide a foundation, but they were not designed for the operational requirements of marine bunkering, which demands speed, reliability, and proximity to berths that fertiliser logistics do not require. Converting or extending these facilities for marine use requires investment in specialised transfer equipment, enhanced safety systems, exclusion zone protocols, and emergency response infrastructure that most port authorities have not yet committed.

Rotterdam and Singapore, the two ports with the most developed frameworks for alternative fuel bunkering, have both published ammonia bunkering roadmaps and are running pilot programmes. Singapore's simulation work on ammonia dispersion scenarios has directly informed the safety protocols that port users must comply with. Rotterdam's extensive hydrogen and ammonia import terminal development is oriented primarily toward the fertiliser and industrial markets but is generating the infrastructure base that marine bunkering will need. Neither port has yet delivered ammonia bunkering as a routine commercial service available to any vessel that requests it.

For ports outside the North Sea and Singapore, the timeline is less clear. The IMO's Interim Guidelines for the Safety of Ships Using Ammonia as Fuel, published in 2025, establish the framework for flag state approval and design requirements, but they do not create the bunkering infrastructure that vessels arriving at a port require. A dual-fuel vessel capable of running on ammonia but unable to bunker at its destination effectively becomes a diesel vessel, negating the investment premium paid for its ammonia capability.

This infrastructure gap is the most immediate practical constraint on ammonia adoption in 2026. It is also, given the long lead times of port investment, the gap that requires the most urgent policy attention.

What a Cargo Owner Actually Pays

For Brazilian exporters, the ammonia transition is not yet a cost line on a freight invoice. It is a regulatory and market trajectory that will determine what ocean freight costs in the decade ahead.

More than 80 per cent of cargo owners surveyed by BCG indicate a willingness to pay a premium for green shipping services, with an average willingness to pay of approximately 4 per cent. The premium required to make green ammonia commercially viable for operators in the early years of transition is estimated at between 10 and 15 per cent. That gap is not primarily a problem of cargo owner resistance. It is a problem of regulatory framework: the incentive structure that makes 4 per cent expressed willingness become 10 to 15 per cent actual market premium requires the carbon levies, FuelEU penalties, and contract-for-difference mechanisms to translate regulatory intent into freight rate signals.

As IMO carbon pricing takes effect from 2028, and as EU ETS costs continue to rise, the economics of fuel choice will shift. A vessel running on VLSFO on a European route from Santos will face carbon costs that a vessel running on green ammonia does not. That differential will appear in the commercial negotiations between Brazilian exporters and the carriers they use. The trajectory is clear even if the exact timeline remains contested.

The Judgment the Industry Must Make Now

Shipping operates on long lead times. A vessel ordered today will be in service for 25 years. An engine platform reaching commercial maturity in 2026 will power vessels that are still sailing in 2051. The regulatory targets set for 2050 are not distant ambitions to be addressed by the next generation of executives; they are the operational environment that ships ordered in 2026 will be required to navigate throughout their working lives.

The Antwerpen's departure from South Korea in June 2026 was one ship. It is the leading edge of what the Ammonia Energy Association counts as approximately 140 vessels on the global ammonia-powered orderbook, with deliveries concentrating in the window between now and 2028. The engine manufacturers have their products. The regulators have their frameworks. The fuel producers are building capacity. The safety protocols are being written, tested, and refined with each successive bunkering trial.

What remains is the hardest part: the simultaneous scaling of production, infrastructure, training, and commercial frameworks across an industry that has historically changed slowly, in a timeframe that the physics of climate change has made non-negotiable.

Ammonia is dangerous. It is also, on the available evidence, indispensable. The gamble the industry is now making is not whether to bet on ammonia. Several major shipowners and engine manufacturers have already placed that bet, with steel and cash. The gamble is whether the regulatory consistency, infrastructure investment, and commercial incentives required to make ammonia viable at scale will arrive in time for those bets to pay off.

The Antwerpen is at sea. The answer is still being written.

title: NGOs Call on IMO Member States to ignore Dangerous Distractions En Route to Net Zero
description:
Those threats have now materialized in the form of ‘alternative’ proposals from a number of IMO member states.
The IMO already delayed its planned timetable of establishing a climate framework for global shipping in 2025, by adjourning MEPC ES.2 for a year.
“Both proposals are designed to placate those that do not think shipping climate action is needed, and serve only to undermine what has been achieved so far.
The result is supported by a comprehensive impact assessment, and has the ability to deliver on the goals of the IMO GHG Strategy”.
Now is the moment for the IMO and all its member states to have the courage to protect and adopt the Net-Zero Framework ‘as is’”, concluded Leppert.
text:
LONDON: Ahead of next week’s key meeting of the International Maritime Organization (IMO), the Clean Shipping Coalition is calling on member states to hold firm in their support for the Net-Zero Framework (NZF) – the UN shipping body’s long negotiated compromise climate agreement – in the face of “alternative proposals” that seek to undermine climate action by the shipping sector.

“While less ambitious than we had hoped for, the NZF’s broad political support from member states means it remains the best tool available to meet the IMO’s Greenhouse Gas Strategy goals on climate, decarbonisation and a just and equitable energy transition for the shipping industry, and must be adopted by the IMO this December”, said Clean Shipping Coalition President Lukas Leppert. “The result of multiple rounds of negotiations, the NZF is already by any measure, an acceptable compromise. Any further weakening would lead to a less effective, slower, and costlier transition”.

The shipping sector makes up 2-3% of global greenhouse gas emissions – comparable to the world’s fifth biggest emitting country, Japan. The IMO has committed to achieving its GHG Strategy goal, including its long-term goal of decarbonisation by 2050, its interim targets of a 30% reduction in absolute emissions by 2030 and 80% by 2040, and its commitment to a just and equitable transition.

Discussions during ISWG-GHG 22 (Intersessional Working Group on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships in London, 1-4 September) are expected to include IMO’s long negotiated compromise agreement, the Net-Zero Framework (NZF), and its proposed adoption at December’s Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC 85/ES.2). Approved during MEPC 83 in 2025, the NZF includes a “global fuel standard” (GFS), which requires ship operators to gradually decrease the amount of greenhouse gas emitted by shipping fuels – or pay penalties. The framework also introduces a mechanism that puts a price on a portion of greenhouse gases ships emit, giving the industry a clear financial incentive to reduce emissions in line with the global fuel standard. See also: IMO paper on the NZF – MEPC 85/3/8: Consideration And Adoption of Amendments to Mandatory Instruments: Amendments to MARPOL Annex VI.

“Shipping is the backbone of the global economy, with estimates of shipping trade’s market value topping $14 trillion, but as it’s also a major source of climate pollution, heating up our ocean and our planet, it must be part of the solution”, said Delaine McCullough, Shipping Program Director at Ocean Conservancy. “As ocean temperatures hit record highs again this summer, increasing storm intensity and threatening marine life, food supplies, and coastal communities, there’s no time for further delay in addressing the roughly one billion tons of carbon dioxide shipping spews into our atmosphere every year.”

“It’s taken years of negotiating and compromise by IMO member states to get to the Net-Zero Framework (NZF)”, added McCullough. “It may not be perfect, but it has the elements needed to eliminate the global shipping industry’s emissions by 2050 and help ensure that the countries facing the greatest climate risks with the least capacity to respond are not further harmed in the maritime energy transition. Adoption of the NZF ‘as is’ would be a huge step forward for our climate, communities, and ocean.”

“The Clean Shipping Coalition cannot support any option that does not include a financial GHG emission penalty and fund”, said Sönke Diesener, Senior Policy Officer Maritime Transport at NABU. “These economic measures are essential for incentivizing emission reductions, supporting the uptake of zero-emission fuels and technologies as well as for ensuring a just and equitable transition. The sector requires clear regulatory directions for the transition and the IMO now has the opportunity to deliver global planning security for the ramp-up of sustainable solutions.”

Further consideration of the development of the IMO Life Cycle GHG Assessment (LCA) framework which will determine well-to-wake emissions and sustainability criteria for global marine fuels is also included on the ISWG-GHG 22 agenda.

“If the IMO gives an advantage to methane-based fuels such as LNG and biomethane, as current submissions to ISWG are calling for, this would lock in shipping emissions of methane, a super pollutant, for decades to come”, said Andrew Dumbrille, Co-Director, Equal Routes. “The LCA guidelines must include sustainability criteria that account for biodiversity and human rights impacts, real world emissions factors for methane-based fuels, and reflect GHG emissions of indirect land use change caused by production of biogenic fuels.”

“With accelerated climate warming already driving devastating impacts around the world, such as record heatwaves, flooding, wildfires and droughts, there is no doubt that the industry must rapidly lower its greenhouse gas emissions”, said Anaïs Rios, Senior Shipping Policy Officer at Seas At Risk. “For the shipping sector, the question is no longer whether it needs to decarbonise, but how best to meet the goals of the International Maritime Organization’s (IMO) GHG (greenhouse gas) Strategy and to reach net zero by 2050. The industry must quickly evolve so that it acts as a shared good for people, rather than a key contributor to the climate crisis and the loss of health and livelihoods around the world. The best way to achieve this is for IMO member states to adopt the Net-Zero Framework in December.”

Following widespread support for the NZF at MEPC 84 in May 20226, the Clean Shipping Coalition stated that “IMO’s Net-Zero Framework is back on track”, but that supporters must remain “vigilant and strong in order to parry inevitable future attacks and attempts to further delay the process of adoption, which is scheduled for early December”.

Those threats have now materialized in the form of ‘alternative’ proposals from a number of IMO member states. Having analysed the available proposals, the Clean Shipping Coalition has found two of them particularly unfit for decarbonization: those submitted by Liberia and Japan. (The other proposals are covered in the notes below.)

Liberia

Instead of setting reduction targets on a path to net zero, the submission from Liberia – the world’s largest flag state – would allow ships to stick to conventional fuels if they think cleaner alternatives are too costly or unavailable.

Additionally, Liberia’s proposal puts greater emphasis on trading of surplus units, while removing the idea of mandatory payments into a Net-Zero Fund. Without reduction targets or financial incentives, this would not cause a shift in the shipping sector beyond business-as-usual, while the lack of available funds would make it impossible to address disproportionately negative impacts on states.

“By failing to ensure a just and equitable transition on top of its poor climate performance, the Clean Shipping Coalition finds that Liberia’s proposal constitutes a fundamental redesign which will fail to deliver on the goals set out in the 2023 IMO Greenhouse Gas Strategy”, said Leppert.

Japan

Japan’s proposal would fundamentally fail to deliver on the goals set out in the GHG Strategy 2023. Japan has put forward a questionable alternative to compliance payments flowing into a centralized fund, which would allow shipowners to direct payments to projects of their own choice.

“Without proper oversight from a governing board, and a clearer focus, the system proposed by Japan risks creating a scheme where money is invested into projects that do little to reduce emissions”, said Alex Springer, Interim Shipping Director at T&E. “Left to its own devices, the industry will continue its reliance on dead-end ‘solutions’ like fossil LNG or crop biofuels, for an expensive, long-term fossil lock-in. Real solutions such as e-fuels and electrification require investment certainty, long-term targets, and robust governance – all of which the proposal is lacking.”

The Clean Shipping Coalition is calling for a central fund administered by the IMO or another independent body and sufficient contributions to ensure a just and equitable transition. In order to leave no one behind, states facing disproportionately negative impacts like small island developing states and least developed countries need financial support – which they made abundantly clear at previous negotiations. Japan’s proposal would clearly fail to deliver, haemorrhaging support from one group of states in an attempt to appease another.

Japan’s proposal also carries serious procedural risks. As it was not circulated six months ahead of the meeting (as is the normal requirement), it cannot be adopted under normal rules at MEPC 85.

The IMO already delayed its planned timetable of establishing a climate framework for global shipping in 2025, by adjourning MEPC ES.2 for a year. This delay has wasted time as the planet warms, emissions of greenhouse gases from global shipping continue unhindered, and delayed investments will lead to a hastier and in turn costlier transition. By diverting attention from circulated proposals the submission from Japan risks throwing the IMO further off-course, and would provoke a loss of trust in the organisation’s capacity to police international shipping and deliver on its own goals.

“Both the Liberia and Japan proposals are wrecking balls – aimed at the heart of shipping climate action, and will prevent necessary action, cause higher total costs, will not support a just and equitable transition, and ultimately will fail to meet the obligations the shipping sector faces”, said Leppert. “Both proposals are designed to placate those that do not think shipping climate action is needed, and serve only to undermine what has been achieved so far. Getting to the Net-Zero Framework is the result of multiple years of negotiations. The result is supported by a comprehensive impact assessment, and has the ability to deliver on the goals of the IMO GHG Strategy”.

“Forget the distractions. Now is the moment for the IMO and all its member states to have the courage to protect and adopt the Net-Zero Framework ‘as is’”, concluded Leppert.

Notes: Other alternative proposals

Brazil Proposal

Brazil’s proposal at best can be seen as a weakened version of the NZF: it delivers fewer GHG reductions in the short term, is associated with higher total costs of the transition due to a later kickoff and steeper targets from 2040, and will not gather sufficient financial contributions at the outset. Furthermore, success of delivering a just and equitable transition hinges on the concrete configuration of the proposed “facility” and whether it will be able to support countries facing disproportionately negative impacts or just become an empty shell. Overall, as Brazil’s proposal presents a weaker and overall costlier version of the NZF, which itself is a compromise that doesn’t achieve the IMO’s own GHG strategy, the NZF should be favoured over the Brazil proposal.

text:
Public support for green shipping is spreading across major regions. But governments are taking noticeably different routes to get low- and zero-emission fuels and vessels into commercial use.

Several European nations are building out different links of the supply chain at once, from fuel production to vessels and bunker infrastructure.

For instance, Germany opened applications this month for the first call under a new inland shipping programme, with up to €70 million ($82 million) available for green inland shipping corridors, covering vessel conversions, renewable hydrogen and electricity production and storage, as well as charging and alternative-fuel bunkering infrastructure.

Norway’s Enova has similarly backed both sides of the supply-demand equation. It awarded NOK 344 million ($36 million) to LH2 Shipping for hydrogen-powered vessels in June, and NOK 442 million ($46 million) to Azane Infrastructure for three ammonia bunker terminals last December.

The Netherlands is concentrating €103 million ($120 million) of state aid on renewable methanol- and renewable hydrogen-powered newbuilds and retrofits between 2027 and 2031.

Finland has gone further upstream, awarding investment tax credits of up to €118.6 million ($138 million) to ETFuels Finland for its planned 110,000 mt/year e-methanol plant, with output intended for shipping and industrial customers.

Two Asian programmes focus more squarely on getting cleaner vessels onto the water.

Japan has opened applications under a five-year, JPY 15.1 billion ($95 million) programme to subsidise equipment for hydrogen-, ammonia-, methanol- and battery-powered ships, with JPY 1.2 billion (around $8 million) budgeted for this year. Hydrogen-, ammonia- and battery-powered vessels can receive support covering up to half of eligible costs, compared with one-third for methanol and hybrid vessels. Oceangoing ships qualify only if they run on hydrogen or ammonia.

Hong Kong has earmarked around HK$34 million (around $4 million) for three-year schemes offering port-dues concessions to vessels powered by, bunkering or transporting approved alternative fuels, alongside incentives for alternative-fuelled ships registered under its flag.

Meanwhile, North American support is more piecemeal for now, split between individual ports, infrastructure projects and proposed federal funding.

Québec has committed around CAD 5 million ($3.5 million) to install shore power at the Port of Québec.

The Port of Long Beach is offering $1 million to the first oceangoing vessel to bunker methanol on a “commercial scale” at the US port.

The port authority estimates that a methanol bunker call currently costs around $1.5 million, compared with roughly $1 million for conventional marine fuels. Half of the award is therefore intended to cover that estimated $500,000 difference. The remainder would help cover ancillary expenses such as permitting and new operational and safety procedures.

A much larger US intervention has been proposed but has yet to materialise.

US representatives Nanette Barragán and Troy Carter, along with senator Chris Van Hollen, reintroduced the Next Generation Shipping Act in June. The bill proposes $1 billion/year for zero-emission-potential vessels, retrofits, research and clean-fuel and charging infrastructure. “The bill would also help the United States keep up with other countries in Europe and Asia that are already investing heavily in clean shipping technology,” the lawmakers wrote in a joint statement.

Other governments have started the legwork without reaching for their pockets yet.

Egyptian authorities have assessed low- and zero-emission fuel production, storage and bunkering potential at five ports under the IMO’s GreenVoyage2050 programme. The assessment came with no funding announcement, but the work is intended to identify infrastructure, regulatory and safety requirements and help attract future investment.

These regional approaches may differ, but they are increasingly addressing the same chicken-and-egg problem from different directions. Shipowners are reluctant to invest without affordable fuels and reliable infrastructure, and clean-fuel producers and infrastructure developers need enough demand to justify their own investments.

Public funding can help break that deadlock by lowering the upfront cost and investment risk on both sides until the market can support itself.

In other alt fuels news this week, nuclear technology company Core Power has signed an agreement with the US Department of Transportation’s Maritime Administration (MARAD) to establish a pathway for US-flagged nuclear-powered merchant vessels, with construction of the first ships targeted to begin in 2028.

Indian state-owned gas utility GAIL, Deendayal Port Authority and classification society DNV have signed an agreement to explore the development of an LNG bunkering facility at Kandla Port.

text:
As the shipping industry moves towards cleaner solutions, the Port of Klaipėda is preparing for changing market needs. Stricter environmental requirements and the growing market for alternative fuels mean that ports need to start planning now for the infrastructure and services that will be needed in the future. Together with its partners, the Klaipėda Port Authority has assessed the potential for green methanol bunkering and developed a concept for a vessel that could provide this service.

“The energy transition is changing the maritime sector and creating demand for cleaner solutions. As the alternative fuels market develops, ports will also need to adapt their infrastructure and services. We are preparing now so that, as green shipping corridors develop across the Baltic Sea, the Port of Klaipėda will be ready to meet market needs and remain competitive. Green methanol bunkering has real potential both in Klaipėda and across the Baltic Sea region,” says Algis Latakas, CEO of the Klaipėda Port Authority.

The Port Authority explored new solutions for cleaner shipping together with 14 partners from different countries through the H2Deri@BSP project. The project aims to accelerate the use of hydrogen-based fuels and support the transition towards zero-emission shipping.

As part of the project, the Klaipėda Port Authority assessed the Port’s potential to offer green methanol bunkering services in the future. The study looked at expected demand for green methanol, regulations supporting the use of alternative fuels, potential customers and fuel supply chains, as well as the environmental benefits of green methanol.

An analysis by Moffatt & Nichol Baltics found that although the green methanol market in the Baltic region is still at an early stage, ports that can offer alternative fuel bunkering are likely to become increasingly attractive to shipping lines. For Klaipėda, green methanol bunkering could also become a new business area, bringing additional revenue and expanding the range of services available at the Port.

The study also identified potential for green methanol to be produced from green hydrogen in the future. The Port of Klaipėda already has a green hydrogen production facility in operation. As the shipping industry works towards its decarbonisation goals, green methanol could see particularly strong demand from regional vessels, passenger ships and ferries, as well as vessels serving offshore wind farms.

The Port of Klaipėda continues to strengthen its role as an energy port. Since 2024, the green methanol-powered container ship Eco Umande, operated by Singapore’s X-Press Feeders, has been calling at the Port of Klaipėda. The Port has also signed a cooperation agreement with several other ports to support the development of green methanol infrastructure. Offering green methanol bunkering services could therefore further strengthen Klaipėda’s competitiveness and create new opportunities for the Port.

The project has already moved beyond analysis to a practical solution. The project developed a technical specification and concept design for a green methanol bunkering vessel for the Port of Klaipėda.The concept was developed by Western Baltic Engineering, part of the Western Shipyard Group (VLG) operating at the Port of Klaipėda.

text:
Critical Talks Resume at IMO Headquarters

Delegates from member states will gather in London next week for a pivotal session of the International Maritime Organization (IMO) to advance discussions on the Net-Zero Framework for international shipping. The negotiations, set to run from [insert dates if available], will focus on key regulatory measures aimed at decarbonizing the maritime sector by 2050.

Carbon Pricing Remains a Contentious Issue

The most divisive topic on the agenda is the proposed implementation of a carbon pricing mechanism. While some nations advocate for a global levy on greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions to incentivize low-carbon fuels and technologies, others argue that such a measure could disproportionately impact developing economies and smaller flag states.

Proponents of carbon pricing emphasize its potential to accelerate the adoption of alternative fuels, such as ammonia, hydrogen, and methanol, while generating revenue for green shipping initiatives. Critics, however, warn of potential market distortions and increased operational costs for vessel operators, particularly in regions with limited access to zero-emission technologies.

Alternative Proposals and Compromise Efforts

In addition to carbon pricing, discussions will cover a range of complementary measures, including:

Fuel standards: Mandating the use of low-carbon or zero-emission fuels through phased regulations.

Energy efficiency targets: Strengthening the IMO’s existing Energy Efficiency Existing Ship Index (EEXI) and Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII) requirements.

Research and development funding: Establishing a global R&D fund to support the development of scalable decarbonization technologies.

Market-based measures (MBMs): Exploring hybrid approaches, such as emissions trading systems or rebate mechanisms, to balance economic and environmental objectives.

Several delegations are expected to push for a compromise framework that combines elements of carbon pricing with targeted exemptions or subsidies for vulnerable economies. The outcome of these negotiations will shape the trajectory of global shipping’s transition to net-zero emissions.

Industry and Stakeholder Engagement

Maritime industry associations, environmental groups, and classification societies will closely monitor the proceedings, with many calling for a clear, equitable, and enforceable regulatory pathway. The IMO’s ability to reconcile divergent national interests while maintaining the sector’s competitiveness will be critical to achieving its ambitious decarbonization goals.

Further updates will be provided as negotiations progress.

title: The Caribbean Isn't Out of Moves on the IMO's Net-Zero Framework - St. Lucia Times
description:
By Kerrlene Wills The Caribbean voice has never been louder and more present in discussions that decide the future of global shipping.
When I first took part in the UN’s International Maritime Organisation (IMO) negotiations on maritime decarbonisation in London in 2022, Caribbean countries were largely absent from the room.
This is especially through initiatives like the Caribbean Shipping Lanes Project (CSL), which brings together regional academic institutions and bodies to contribute to a collective voice for the Caribbean Community (CARICOM).
But from my experience working with a Caribbean shipping company, I know we need to plan carefully so that our most vulnerable groups don’t end up carrying the biggest burdens.
I hope these four suggestions help move the discussion forward constructively and in a way that benefits the Caribbean.
text:
By Kerrlene Wills

The Caribbean voice has never been louder and more present in discussions that decide the future of global shipping. As negotiations reach a boiling point this year, the region still has four ways to influence the outcome.

When I first took part in the UN’s International Maritime Organisation (IMO) negotiations on maritime decarbonisation in London in 2022, Caribbean countries were largely absent from the room.

Considering how consequential the discussions would be for a region so dependent on shipping, it soon became my mission to help ensure that the Caribbean’s voice is heard in the design of what would become the Net-Zero Framework (NZF), the IMO’s flagship climate policy.

Some said it could not be done. But after three years of intensive work with partners on the ground, the region is fully engaged in the discussions. This is especially through initiatives like the Caribbean Shipping Lanes Project (CSL), which brings together regional academic institutions and bodies to contribute to a collective voice for the Caribbean Community (CARICOM).

Now, our voices are being heard.

Through my work, I saw firsthand what decarbonisation would mean for shipping in the region, including challenges like fuel availability, infrastructure limits and whether certain routes would still work.

As IMO talks now reach a second act nobody expected, the region has a unique opportunity to fine-tune the NZF design to ensure essential goods continue to move across the region while we cut emissions.

From my perspective, four key principles need to be included in the NZF to make this happen.

Emphasise Just and Equitable Transition (JET)

The universal levy proposed by over 50 countries in 2025 was, in my view, the best approach to decarbonisation because it was simple and made every ship contribute.

With the two-tiered NZF compromise agreed last year, the costs of decarbonisation now fall more heavily on certain ships, many of which work in already vulnerable markets like the Caribbean. This means the ships least able to change are facing the highest costs.

As a result, resources devoted to JET need to be stronger, not weaker. This is especially important because developing countries would, in many cases, be the ones paying into the system. Funding is needed to address the financial access, infrastructure, technology, fuel and capacity constraints that make decarbonisation disproportionately difficult for developing markets.

We cannot abandon the NZF’s JET principles and deep decarbonisation.

Introduce a targeted mechanism for structurally constrained shipping

Vessels in structurally constrained networks, such as those in the Caribbean, face real operational challenges to decarbonisation. Under the current structure of the NZF, the pool of funding available to support zero-emission fuel adoption and address these challenges is insufficient and is already under political pressure to shrink further.

I don’t think the answer is to lower the ambition of the entire Framework to meet the lowest common denominator for decarbonization. What good is a multilateral agreement that simply preserves business as usual?

But from my experience working with a Caribbean shipping company, I know we need to plan carefully so that our most vulnerable groups don’t end up carrying the biggest burdens.

First, we must ensure that resources are made available to keep the IMO’s promise that “no country is left behind”.

We can also consider how vulnerable stakeholders might keep resources in their region and avoid some of the worst impacts of these measures. Where transition capital is limited and alternative fuels may not be available, addressing “disproportionate negative impacts” might mean credits or compliance relief, in addition to financial support or adjustment assistance.

Preserve the economic signal and reward genuine first movers

If we want companies to invest early in zero- and near-zero-emission technologies, we need to reward them for taking that risk.

LNG and other fossil pathways may have a transitional role, as contemplated in some proposals on the NZF. However, transitional does not mean reward-eligible. Fossil fuel pathways already receive financing from national coffers.

Funds generated by the NZF should instead contribute to scaling the technologies and fuels needed for long-term decarbonisation, achieve the agreement’s objectives, and meet the agreed targets.

I still think most of the funding should help developing countries join the decarbonisation effort and tackle the barriers they face. Even so, a reward system is important to encourage innovation and support those willing to take early risks to break the cycle of high costs, low investment, and limited fuel options.

Give commercial actors a voice – but not the entire purse

Finally, I understand the logic behind proposals calling for greater shipowner control over where contributions go. Shipowners know where the infrastructure gaps are and what the challenges are for decarbonising their fleets, especially for regional operators.

But we all know that ultimately costs flow through freight rates to consumers. The governance of transition finance has to reflect those broader interests as well.

I would favour a public-private model, with meaningful shipowner participation and government oversight and involvement in project design, so that financing tackles the immediate challenges to getting decarbonisation off the ground.

Ultimately, the future of the Framework will be decided in December. I hope these four suggestions help move the discussion forward constructively and in a way that benefits the Caribbean.

My biggest hope is that the region gets the best possible deal from this process – one that protects our interests, encourages innovation in clean and renewable energy, and most importantly, leads to real cuts in emissions.

text:
The Union of Greek Shipowners (UGS) wants emission targets determined by what the bunker market can actually supply, ahead of IMO talks on 1 September.

IMAGE: Delegates at the IMO's Marine Environment Protection Committee's Extraordinary Session (MEPC ES.2), which ran between 13-17 October 2025 in London. Flickr of the IMO

The UGS said the currently approved NZF has "significant weaknesses" and called for a global framework that combines emissions reductions with economic viability.

It argued that global shipping regulations need to take greater account of whether alternatives to conventional fuels can be supplied in sufficient volumes and at viable prices.

Against this backdrop, it has backed the Panama-Liberia approach as a "balanced and pragmatic foundation" for further negotiations, arguing that it better reflects practical constraints around alternative marine fuel supply and cost.

It also welcomed the proposal's greater emphasis on vessel energy efficiency, arguing that efficiency improvements will remain particularly important while suitable alternative fuels are either unavailable or prohibitively expensive.

Liberia submitted the proposal to MEPC 85 alone, building on a proposal by Argentina, Liberia and Panama considered at MEPC 84. It would remove GHG pricing from the framework and instead set GHG Fuel Intensity (GFI) reduction targets based on the affordability, availability and scalability of low-emission fuels. The trajectory would be reviewed for revision every five years.

It would rely on surplus units (SUs) as the sole compliance mechanism. Ships performing better than their GFI target could generate units that other vessels could use, while units could also be banked or borrowed from up to two consecutive years.

The UGS also pointed to Japan's proposal as recognising some of the challenges surrounding future fuel supply.

Japan has put forward a basis for discussion seeking to soften GFI reduction targets from 2030 onwards while replacing payments into the Net-Zero Fund with a "direct contribution" mechanism.

Instead of purchasing remedial units, shipowners could either buy surplus units to cover non-compliance or contribute directly to projects proposed by member states and approved by the MEPC.

“Ambitious targets, however, need to remain realistic, and go hand in hand with solutions that reflect technological capabilities and the realities of the global market,” said UGS president Melina Travlos. The Liberian proposal received support from several IMO member states, including Oman, Kuwait, Jordan, Somalia, Yemen and Tunisia, during MEPC 84 discussions. But several other member states and climate groups, including Opportunity Green, have strongly opposed removing GHG pricing.

Proposals by Tuvalu, ACSA-UK, Brazil and Liberia will now be debated at the IMO's intersessional GHG working group meetings in September and November, before delegates consider the framework at MEPC 85 from 30 November to 3 December.

If member states agree on a final text, the amendments could then be formally adopted at MEPC ES.2, expected to reconvene on 4 December.

Meanwhile, Japan's proposal was submitted on 20 July, which was after the 30 May deadline for circulating draft amendments six months before MEPC 85.
